articles.title: In the Time It Takes to Blink
articles.dek: Paul promised the resurrection wouldn't creep in like dawn — it would arrive complete, in an instant, the way New York's first electric night refused to happen gradually.
articles.quote: Death isn't defeated slowly. It's swallowed up in an instant — the way the dark didn't fade over Manhattan, it disappeared the moment the switch went up.
articles.body:
On the evening of September 4, 1882, a small crowd gathered in the office of financier J. P. Morgan on Wall Street, waiting to see something no one alive had ever witnessed. Thomas Edison stood beside a switch. Skeptics filled the room too — bankers who had bet on gas, engineers who doubted a citywide grid could ever hold together without fire or failure. At three o'clock that afternoon, at Edison's signal, four hundred lightbulbs strung through offices and streets across a one-square-mile stretch of lower Manhattan came on — not gradually, not one at a time, but together, in the same instant. Until that day, cities fought the dark the slow way. A lamplighter walked from post to post at dusk, touching a flame to each gas lamp, working down one street and then the next, so a neighborhood eased into light block by block over the better part of an hour. Pearl Street Station ended that argument for good. The skeptics in the room went quiet. Darkness didn't fade that afternoon. It was switched off.

Paul had something far bigger than a power grid in mind when he wrote to the church in Corinth, but he reached for a similar kind of picture. Some believers there were stuck on an honest, uncomfortable question: if the body dies, how could it possibly live again, and what would that even look like (1 Cor 15:35)? Many Corinthians had grown up steeped in Greek thought, which prized the soul and treated the body as a shell best escaped, not something worth rescuing. A resurrected body sounded, to them, like a downgrade. Paul doesn't scold them for asking. He answers with the most ordinary thing in the world: a seed. Drop a seed into the ground, he says, and it doesn't stay a seed. It dies, and out of that death comes something the seed never resembled on its own (1 Cor 15:36-38). What's planted is perishable, weak, sown in dishonor, headed for decay. What comes up is imperishable, powerful, raised in glory (1 Cor 15:42-44). Death, Paul is saying, isn't the opposite of life, and it isn't an escape from the body either. It's the doorway into a far better one.

Then he does something remarkable. He stops reasoning and starts unveiling. Listen, I tell you a mystery, he writes, pulling back a curtain on something no philosopher in Corinth could have argued his way to. Not everyone will die before Christ returns, he says, but everyone will be changed. And notice the detail worth slowing down on: he doesn't describe that change unfolding gradually, the way a caterpillar spends its slow, hidden weeks inside a chrysalis, or the way a wound closes a little more every day. He reaches for the fastest image his language has.

"We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed—in a flash, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." (1 Corinthians 15:51-52)

A flash. A blink. Quicker than a lamplighter can strike a single match, let alone walk a street. Notice what Paul does not say here. He does not say death fades, erodes, or gets slowly out-lived. He says it will be swallowed. Death isn't defeated slowly. It's swallowed up in an instant — the way the dark didn't fade over Manhattan, it disappeared the moment the switch went up. If the resurrection arrived gradually, a little more each generation, a little more with each medical breakthrough, we might picture it as one more slow improvement, something humanity could eventually manage on its own patience and progress, the way we've learned to manage pain or delay aging. But Paul insists this isn't an upgrade we earn by waiting well. It's a gift that lands all at once, from outside, on a day only God has scheduled.

That's what makes the next line the loudest note in the whole letter. Paul reaches back into the prophets and throws the taunt every grieving person has ever wanted to throw.

"Death has been swallowed up in victory." "Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?" (1 Corinthians 15:54-55)

Swallowed up. Not worn down after a long campaign. Not dimmed. Swallowed — the way darkness over lower Manhattan wasn't gradually diminished but erased the second the current hit the filaments. For a Filipino reader, that's worth sitting with, because so much of our faith gets lived in the meantime: waiting for test results, waiting for a visa, waiting out a wake that stretches on for days while relatives arrive from the province one by one, waiting by a hospital bed for news that doesn't come as fast as we'd like. We're used to hoping things get better slowly, the way a fever finally breaks or a debt finally gets paid down. Paul isn't offering that kind of hope here. He's promising a specific, sudden, guaranteed event — a trumpet, a blink, and death, the one thing every culture on earth has feared since the beginning, undone in less time than it takes to say the word.

That's not a reason to grieve carelessly, or rush past a funeral, or pretend the waiting doesn't ache. Paul knew grief himself, well enough to write whole letters about it. He also knew that grief was not the end of the story he was telling. It's a reason to keep standing while you wait. Paul doesn't end the chapter with theology. He ends it with instructions.

"Therefore, my dear brothers and sisters, stand firm. Let nothing move you. Always give yourselves fully to the work of the Lord, because you know that your labor in the Lord is not in vain." (1 Corinthians 15:58)

Notice that last phrase. Not in vain. Every quiet act of faithfulness you offer while you wait — the patience with a difficult parent, the prayer prayed again for the same request, the honest day's work nobody claps for — is not wasted effort scattered into the dark. It's stored up for the moment the switch goes up, and not one bit of it will be forgotten.

Whatever this week is asking of you — a hard diagnosis, a long shift, a grief that hasn't lifted yet — you are not waiting for the dark to fade slowly. You are waiting for a switch. So keep laboring. Keep loving the people in front of you. Keep standing, because none of it will be lost when the light comes on. And when it does, it won't creep in one lamp at a time. It will be a flash. A blink. And everything that ever looked like an ending will simply, suddenly, be over.

articles.title: The Seed That Sails Without a Map
articles.dek: A coconut can't see the shore it's drifting toward — and neither can you. Ecclesiastes 11 says sow anyway.
articles.quote: You are not responsible for the tide. You are only responsible for the sowing.
articles.body:
On August 27, 1883, the island of Krakatoa in the Sunda Strait tore itself apart. The eruption was so violent it was heard nearly 3,000 miles away, in Perth, Australia. Ash blotted out the sun. Tsunamis scraped the coastlines of Java and Sumatra clean. When scientists finally reached what was left of the island, they found nothing alive. Not a blade of grass. Not an insect. The land was sterile rock and ash, a world reset to zero.

Within three years, grass had returned, carried in by wind and birds. But among the first plants to take hold on that dead island were coconut palms, grown from coconuts that had drifted in on the current, sometimes for hundreds of miles, sometimes for months, tossed by storms and salt spray, until they finally washed ashore and, against every likelihood, sprouted. The trees that fed the first generation of life back onto Krakatoa were planted by coconuts whose parent trees were islands away, and would never know what became of them.

Coconuts are built for this kind of journey. Their thick, fibrous husk is not decoration, it is a life raft. It traps air, so the seed floats. It is waterproof and shock absorbent, so the embryo inside can survive months at sea, drifting on ocean currents with no say in where it lands. Scientists have tracked coconuts floating over 100 days and thousands of miles, from one shoreline to another, before germinating. The tree never sees where its fruit finally takes root. It sows, and lets go.

That is the picture running underneath one of the most practical passages in the Bible. Ecclesiastes was written by the Teacher, likely Solomon, near the end of a long life spent testing everything: pleasure, wealth, work, wisdom itself, to see what actually holds up. After chapters of wrestling honestly with how much of life we cannot control, he lands, in chapter 11, on something surprisingly ordinary. Keep working. Keep giving. Keep sowing. Even though, especially though, you cannot see how it ends.

"Ship your grain across the sea; after many days you may receive a return. Invest in seven ventures, yes, in eight; you do not know what disaster may come upon the land." (Ecclesiastes 11:1-2, NIV)

To the Teacher's first readers, this was blunt trade advice. Ancient merchants who shipped grain across the sea had no way of tracking their cargo. No satellite, no insurance claim, no phone call from the captain. They loaded the ship, watched it disappear over the horizon, and waited, sometimes for months, to find out if it made it. Verse 2 pushes further. Do not put everything on one ship. Spread it across seven ventures, or eight, because you cannot see the storm that has not happened yet.

Then, in verse 6, the Teacher makes it personal. "Sow your seed in the morning, and at evening let your hands not be idle, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or whether both will do equally well" (Ecclesiastes 11:6, NIV). Notice what he does not say. He does not say wait until you are sure. He does not say sow only where you know the soil is good. He says sow, morning and evening, both hands, without the guarantee.

Here is what is easy to miss reading this as ancient investment advice. The sowing the Teacher describes is not only about money. Ecclesiastes 11 sits inside a book concerned with what we owe the people around us before the days of trouble come (Ecclesiastes 12:1). Verse 5 even widens the mystery beyond markets and weather. "As you do not know the path of the wind, or how the body is formed in a mother's womb, so you cannot understand the work of God, the Maker of all things" (Ecclesiastes 11:5, NIV). The Teacher is not only talking about grain ships. He is talking about every good thing we release into the world without a guarantee, a kind word, a costly forgiveness, time spent on a child who is not thanking us yet, patience with a marriage that has not turned a corner, a prayer for someone who does not know we are praying it.

That is what makes the coconut such an honest picture of this verse. It does not sow because it can calculate the odds. It sows because sowing is what it was made to do, and the outcome belongs to the current, the wind, and the shore it will never see. Some of what it releases rots in the surf. Some drifts for a season and dies on sand too dry to hold it. And some, like the coconuts that reached Krakatoa, lands on exactly the barren place that needed it most, at exactly the right time, planted by a parent tree that never got to watch it grow.

Filipinos already know a version of this parable, even without a name for it. Walk almost anywhere in the provinces and you will pass a coconut tree older than anyone living near it, planted by a lolo or lola who never lived to see it bear its two hundredth fruit, let alone shade the grandchildren now resting under it at noon. A single niyog can feed a household for generations: oil for the pan, gata for the ginataan, husk for rope and fuel, leaves for the roof. Whoever planted it sowed a working, waiting kind of hope. They dug the hole not knowing who would eat the fruit.

Most of us want the opposite order. We want to see the shore before we let go of the seed. We want proof the marriage will heal before we keep investing in it. We want to know the child will turn out well before we keep showing up at every practice and every parent-teacher conference. We want to know the quiet kindness we did for a stranger mattered before we do it again tomorrow. Ecclesiastes 11 refuses to give us that order. It asks for the sowing first, generous and repeated, both hands, and lets the harvest stay God's business.

This is not a call to be careless. Verse 2's seven ventures, yes eight, is wisdom, not recklessness. Spread your investment of love and effort widely, because you genuinely do not know which relationship, which kindness, which quiet act of faithfulness is the one that will take root. You are not being asked to predict the future. You are being asked to keep your hands from going idle while you wait for a future you cannot predict.

If you are waiting today to see whether something you have sown will ever amount to anything, an apology you keep offering, patience with a difficult parent, a faith you keep quietly living out in front of children who seem uninterested, Ecclesiastes 11 has a word for you. Keep sowing. Pick one seed you can plant today without needing to see it grow: a message you have been meaning to send, a habit of patience you keep choosing, a prayer for someone who will probably never know you prayed it. Let today be the morning sowing, and let tomorrow be the evening one.

You are not responsible for the tide. You are only responsible for the sowing. Somewhere, on a shore you may never see, it is already taking root.

articles.title: The Foundation No One Sees
articles.dek: Psalm 97 says God's throne is wrapped in cloud and darkness — then, in the very next breath, names exactly what it's built on.
articles.quote: You don't have to see through the clouds to trust what's holding up the throne.
articles.body:
In 1870, a crew of workers climbed down an iron shaft into a wooden box the size of a small warehouse, sunk into the mud beneath New York's East River. It was called a caisson, an airtight chamber pumped full of compressed air to hold back the river while men dug toward bedrock by lantern light. They were building the foundation for what would become the Brooklyn Bridge, and not one of them could see it. They worked in a haze of dust and gaslight, sometimes more than seventy feet under a river they couldn't see the surface of, laying stone and concrete for towers that wouldn't rise into daylight for years. Chief engineer Washington Roebling spent so many hours in the caissons that he was left partially paralyzed by what workers then called caisson disease, what we now know as decompression sickness. He finished directing the project from a window overlooking the river, watching through a telescope, sending instructions down through his wife, Emily, because he could no longer walk the site he had designed. But the foundation held. It still holds, more than a century later. Eight million people a year cross the Brooklyn Bridge, and almost none of them ever think about the men who worked in total darkness under the river so the bridge above could stand.

Psalm 97 opens with a coronation shout: "The LORD reigns, let the earth be glad; let the distant shores rejoice" (Psalm 97:1). It's a psalm meant to be read out loud, maybe even shouted, the kind of poetry that wants cymbals and trumpets behind it. Fire goes ahead of God and burns up everything opposing him. Lightning splits the sky so the whole earth can see it. Mountains, the most permanent, unmovable things the psalmist knew, melt like wax in his presence, and all the peoples of the earth see his glory (Psalm 97:3-6). It's a wall of sound, meant to overwhelm, almost too much to take in all at once. And then, right in the middle of all that thunder, the psalm slows down and says something quieter, and stranger, than any of it.

Clouds and thick darkness surround him; righteousness and justice are the foundation of his throne. (Psalm 97:2)

Read that twice. The throne of God, the psalmist says, is wrapped in cloud and thick darkness. He doesn't try to explain that away or apologize for it. There are things about how God rules, how he times things, how he allows what he allows, that stay genuinely hidden from us, no matter how carefully we study or how hard we pray for clarity. Cloud. Darkness. Mystery we don't get to see through, at least not yet. But notice what that very same verse says in its next breath: the foundation underneath all that darkness is not more darkness. It's righteousness and justice. Solid. Named. Specific. The psalmist doesn't claim to know everything about how God's throne operates. But he knows, with complete confidence, exactly what it's standing on.

That's the caisson, isn't it. The men under the East River couldn't see the bridge they were building. They couldn't see Manhattan on one side or Brooklyn on the other, or the ships that would pass beneath the towers, or the carriages and then cars that would one day stream across it by the millions. Their whole world, for months at a time, was dark water, damp timber, and lantern light. But they weren't digging blind. They were digging to a plan drawn up by an engineer who could see the whole bridge in his mind before a single stone was laid. Every foot they cleared was measured, tested, and set in place to bear a weight they would never live to watch cross over their heads. The darkness they worked in was never the absence of a foundation. It was exactly where the foundation got laid.

This is worth sitting with, because most of us don't actually struggle to believe God is powerful. Psalm 97's fire and lightning and melting mountains, most of us can picture that kind of God without much trouble; power has never been the hard part of faith. What we struggle with is verse 2. The cloud. The thick darkness. The parts of our lives where we genuinely cannot see what God is building, a diagnosis with no clear next step, a prayer that's gone unanswered for years, a child who's drifted and hasn't come home yet, a door that closed and hasn't opened onto anything else. Maybe it's an OFW parent still waiting for the papers that will finally let the family reunite, or a small business owner watching the rain come down for the third straight week, wondering if the season will ever turn. We want to see the finished bridge before we'll trust the foundation underneath it. The psalm doesn't offer us that kind of sight. It offers something better and, in the long run, more useful: the foundation is not a mystery, even when everything built on top of it still is.

Righteousness means God does what is right, not what is convenient, not what is fastest, not always what we would choose for ourselves, but what is actually right, all the way down to the bedrock. Justice means the account eventually balances, nothing gets lost in the dark, nothing gets forgotten, nothing stays crooked forever, even when it looks that way from where we're standing. You may not be able to see how God is working in the cloud hanging over your life right now, this week, this diagnosis, this waiting. But you are not left guessing about what holds up his throne while you wait. Scripture names it for you plainly, so you don't have to dig for it yourself, the way Roebling's men had to dig, inch by inch, through mud.

So here's something to keep, maybe write it on a card, maybe just carry it quietly with you today: you don't have to see through the clouds to trust what's holding up the throne. The next time you're waiting on something you can't explain, a job that hasn't come, a diagnosis with no timeline, a marriage or a friendship you're still praying over, you don't need the whole structure to come into view before you're allowed to rest. You just need to know what it's standing on. Roebling's men never got to walk across the bridge they built underwater; most of them moved on to other jobs long before the towers broke the surface. But the work they did in the dark still holds up every footstep that crosses it today. Long before the bridge, someone laid the foundation. Long before your answer arrives, God's righteousness and justice are already in place, steady enough to hold whatever gets built on top, whether or not you ever get to see the plans.

articles.title: The Billionaire Who Gave It All Away
articles.dek: Chuck Feeney spent forty years quietly making other people rich. An old proverb about generosity explains why he never once felt poorer for it.
articles.quote: Whoever refreshes others will be refreshed. Generosity is not a leak in your life — it is a channel for God's blessing to keep moving through you.
articles.body:
In 1982, one of the richest men in the world quietly gave almost everything away — and spent the next four decades making sure almost no one found out. Chuck Feeney had co-founded Duty Free Shoppers, the airport retail chain, and built a personal fortune north of eight billion dollars. Then, without a press release, he signed nearly all of it over to a foundation he had created, Atlantic Philanthropies. For fifteen years, his own business partners had no idea he had become, on paper, one of the poorest billionaires in history. He funded universities, hospitals, and peace efforts from Vietnam to Northern Ireland, always on one condition: his name stayed off the building. He called it "Giving While Living" — he wanted to watch his money do good rather than let a will do it after he was gone. He flew economy class. He wore a fifteen-dollar watch. In his final years he rented a modest apartment in San Francisco — no house, no car, no yacht — because, he said, "you can only wear one pair of shoes at a time." By the time he finished giving, in 2020, Atlantic Philanthropies had distributed more than eight billion dollars, and Feeney kept about two million for himself — not because he ran out, but because that is what he chose to keep. Bill Gates called him "the ultimate example" for a generation of philanthropists who came after him, and said Feeney's model directly inspired the Giving Pledge. Feeney died in 2023, having proven, in the most literal way possible, an old Hebrew proverb written three thousand years before he was born: the one who gives freely ends up richer than the one who holds on.

Long before Chuck Feeney, King Solomon wrote a string of short, sharp sayings about exactly this kind of paradox. Proverbs 11:23–26 is part of a larger collection contrasting two ways to live — one hoarding, one open-handed — and showing where each one actually leads. Solomon opens with a promise: "The desire of the righteous ends only in good, but the hope of the wicked only in wrath" (Proverbs 11:23). Then he gets specific. Verse 26 paints a scene familiar to anyone in the ancient world: a grain merchant sitting on his surplus during a famine, waiting for prices to climb higher before he will sell a single sack. Solomon says plainly, "people curse the one who hoards grain, but blessing crowns the one who is willing to sell" (Proverbs 11:26). Everyone in that community could see exactly who was protecting himself at everyone else's expense, and exactly who was willing to let scarcity cost him something. It was not an abstract principle to them; it was the difference between a neighbor who ate and one who did not. That contrast sets up the line right before it, the one that gives this whole passage its punch.

"One person gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds unduly, but comes to poverty. A generous person will prosper; whoever refreshes others will be refreshed." (Proverbs 11:24–25, NIV)

Read that again slowly, because it does not say what we expect. Common sense says a person who gives money away has less of it. Solomon says the opposite: he "gives freely, yet gains even more." It is worth asking why he would write something that sounds so backwards. Notice the word Solomon chooses for what a generous person does to others: "refreshes." It is a watering word, the kind used for irrigating a parched field. In a dry land like ancient Israel, water poured onto a field was not lost — it was invested. It came back as grain, as fruit, as a harvest big enough to feed the very hand that poured it. That is the picture Solomon is drawing. Generosity, in this proverb, is never a leak in your resources. It is an irrigation channel — one that waters someone else and somehow loops back around and waters you too. Notice also what verse 24 does not say. It does not say the generous person gains back exactly what they gave, dollar for dollar, like a vending machine returning change. It says they gain "even more" — an increase that outpaces the gift. That is not a spreadsheet. It is closer to what a farmer knows in his bones: you do not get back the seed you planted. You get back the harvest. This is not a formula that guarantees a bank balance; Solomon is not promising every generous person a windfall, and Scripture never lets us treat God like a machine we can manipulate with the right amount of giving. It is simply describing how life, under God's design, tends to work. Centuries later, Paul says almost the identical thing to a stingy church in Corinth: "whoever sows generously will also reap generously... God is able to bless you abundantly" (2 Corinthians 9:6, 8).

And behind both the proverb and the promise stands the ultimate proof: God himself. "For God so loved the world that he gave..." (John 3:16) — the whole gospel is God refusing to hoard. Jesus "made himself nothing" on the cross, Paul writes, and God "exalted him to the highest place" (Philippians 2:7, 9) — the very pattern Solomon described a thousand years earlier, playing out on a hill outside Jerusalem. The Son gave everything, and in the resurrection, gained more than anyone could measure. That is the gospel in miniature: grace poured out becomes glory poured back. If you have received that kind of giving — a Savior who emptied himself for you — generosity stops being a discipline you grit your teeth through. It becomes the most natural response there is.

You do not need eight billion dollars to live this out. You need one person this week who is running dry — a coworker who is stretched thin, a relative short on rent, a friend who just needs an hour of your attention — and you need to be willing to pour something toward them before you are sure you can spare it. Pay for someone's meal without making a thing of it. Forgive the small debt you have been quietly keeping score on. Say the encouraging word out loud instead of just thinking it and moving on. Show up for the neighbor whose harvest failed, the way that ancient grain merchant refused to. None of these cost eight billion dollars. All of them cost something real, which is the whole point — a gift that costs nothing is not really a gift.

Solomon is not asking you to be reckless with what God has given you. He is asking you to stop believing that holding on tighter is what keeps you safe. Chuck Feeney spent forty years testing that belief and found it false. Whoever refreshes others will be refreshed. Generosity is not a leak in your life — it is a channel for God's blessing to keep moving through you. This week, open the channel, and see where the water goes.
